vignette:
Arthur Jenkins, at 78, moves through his days with the careful, deliberate pace of a man who has learned that life can turn on a dime. His world, once a meticulous arrangement of data points and logical sequences, feels irrevocably altered. He is a database administrator, a role he's held for decades, and until a year ago, it was a source of quiet pride and predictable order. Now, his days at the office are a constant battle against an unseen enemy within.

It started so suddenly. One Tuesday evening, after a typical day of optimizing queries and troubleshooting server issues, a crushing pressure seized his chest. It wasn't just pain; it was an overwhelming sense of being squeezed, unable to draw a full breath. He remembers the cold sweat, the frantic call to 911, the siren's wail growing louder as paramedics burst through his door. The ride in the ambulance was a blur of flashing lights and urgent voices, a terrifying descent into chaos. He remembers the feeling of losing control, the fear that he was dying right there on the stretcher.

The next week was a nightmare. He woke up in the ICU after emergency triple bypass surgery, disoriented, weak, and tethered to a dozen machines. The constant beeping of monitors, the rhythmic hiss of the ventilator before it was removed, the smell of antiseptic - these sensations are etched into his memory. He recalls the nurses' hushed conversations, the feeling of vulnerability as tubes snaked from his body, and the crushing realization of how close he had come to the precipice. Every cough, every shift in position, brought a sharp, visceral fear that his chest would tear open, that his heart would simply stop.

Now, a year later, the hospital is behind him, but it's never truly gone. The scent of a cleaning product in the office cafeteria can instantly transport him back to the sterile cold of his ICU room, making his breath catch in his throat. A car alarm blaring outside his apartment window often triggers a jolt of panic, his mind twisting the sound into the urgent, high-pitched alerts of a medical monitor. He finds himself constantly checking his pulse, listening intently to his own breathing, convinced that any slight deviation is a sign of impending doom. He avoids medical dramas on television, quickly changing the channel if a hospital scene appears, unable to bear the sight of defibrillators or IV lines.

His once-sharp focus at work is severely compromised. Arthur prides himself on precision, on the elegant logic of his database structures, but now, intrusive thoughts often derail him. He'll be in the middle of writing a complex SQL query, and suddenly, he's replaying the feeling of the nurse inserting a catheter, or the doctor explaining the risks of surgery. These mental intrusions make it difficult to concentrate, leading to uncharacteristic errors in his code and missed deadlines. He spends hours re-checking his work, not out of his usual meticulousness, but out of a desperate, anxious need to regain a sense of control over anything, even if it's just a line of code.

Sleep offers little respite. Nightmares plague him, often involving being trapped, suffocated, or experiencing the intense chest pain all over again. He wakes up in a sweat, his heart pounding, convinced for a moment that he's back in that hospital bed, helpless. He feels a pervasive sense of dread, a belief that his body is a fragile, unreliable machine that could betray him again at any moment. The world, which once seemed orderly and predictable, now feels inherently unsafe. He finds himself irritable, snapping at younger colleagues who ask for help, something he never used to do. He feels distant, estranged from the casual camaraderie of the office, his colleagues' everyday concerns seeming trivial compared to the terror he carries within him. He simply can't connect, feeling a profound sense of isolation, even when surrounded by others.
